publications.description: Research investigating the faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs. Introduces a new causal metric, Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), which reveals that models often produce correct answers despite using post-hoc reasoning. Identifies a specific Reasoning Horizon where causal reliance on reasoning steps decays significantly.

Excited to share that our paper, "Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning," has been accepted to the ICLR (International Conference on Learning Representations) 2026 LIT Workshop! 🎉 As AI systems are deployed in high-stakes settings such as medicine, law, finance, we rely on their explanations to catch errors and verify decisions. But if a model can reach the right answer while ignoring its own stated reasoning, those explanations can't be trusted as a window into its behavior. Transparency tools built on top of flawed reasoning chains may give false confidence to the people relying on them. The core finding: high accuracy doesn't mean a model actually uses its reasoning chain. We introduce NLDD, a metric that measures whether corrupting individual CoT steps changes model confidence, and discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens contribute nothing (or actively hurt). Gemma hit 99% accuracy on logical inference while exhibiting negative NLDD. It was getting the right answer despite its own reasoning, not because of it. Huge thanks to my incredible co-authors Max Loffgren , Om Kotadia , Linus Wong , and mentor Jonas Rohweder — and to Kevin Zhu and the entire Algoverse AI Research team . Doing some research, I stumbled upon Anydoc, a new open-source document parsing engine from Firecrawl , and the performance numbers drew my attention. It's a Rust-based parser for PDFs, DOCX, PPTX, and 10 other document formats, built for local, high-speed parsing. A few highlights: ▫️ Sub-5ms Markdown conversion ▫️ 500 DOCX files parsed in just 1.7 seconds ▫️ Best-in-class quality across 13 document formats ▫️ Built in Rust ▫️ 100% open source This is definitively a game changer If you're building AI agents or working with document-heavy workflows, this looks worth exploring. #OpenSource #RustLang #AI #AIAgents #DocumentAI #LLM #DeveloperTools #PDF #Automation #Firecrawl Nicolas Silberstein Camara Jason Zhou Alex Nucci Bex Tuychiev Caleb Peffer Will Goldfarb Rafael Miller Nicholas Keeley Thomas Kosmas Micah Stairs Rahul Singh Kris Oei Max Loffgren @Neha Patil Gergő Móricz David

Introducing Greptile v5, a ground-up rewrite of the Greptile coding agent. It catches more bugs, with higher precision, and 2x faster (~2 minutes per review) 3 things are better: First, it catches more bugs: We track positive replies like “great catch” and “just fixed” per MR as a proxy for this. v4: 0.266/PR v5: 0.342/PR ∆: 28.6% higher Second, it is higher precision. we track what %age of greptile’s comments are addressed exactly as greptile recommended. this is a very strict way to measure address rate. v4: 52% v5: 66% ∆: 14pp higher Third, it is faster! v4: 5:04 minutes v5: 2:25 minutes ∆: -53%

Last weekend, I had the privilege to attend YC Startup School in San Francisco. While it's not a "school" in a traditional sense, I learned some amazing lessons about today's tech landscape from my class of founders and builders. - Startups aren't bound by software anymore: Some people think that "startup == B2B Saas", but a majority of the demos at Startup School presented robots and hypersonic jets. The world of physical AI is here, and as an EECS student, I'm excited for the opportunity to build an integrated future across hardware and software. - Build from first principles: NVIDIA got started from a textbook on computer graphics. Now it powers AI everywhere. Agents can ship code, but a deep systems understanding is essential. When I build, I combine my knowledge of the fundamentals with a passion for learning how systems work. - Don't make connections, find community: One thing that surprised me at YC was how friendly everyone was. I could wander into a conversation and everyone would pause to introduce themselves and share what they were building. It wasn't phony networking either; people genuinely wanted to help others succeed however they could. At YC, I found friends I'm looking forward to staying in touch with. Speaking of friends, I'm grateful that I spent my Startup School with people like Haley Hernandez , Heba Alazzeh , Lena Conde Araujo , Clemens Helmut Sageder , Humam Al-Shami , Ola Amr and Jasmine Chao . I would also like to thank Gabriel Dupuis and Côme ROSSARY for their cheese suggestions, and Amy Lin and Alex Epstein for the unexpected crossover. Shoutout to Innate and Lightberry for letting me hang out with your stupendous robots. Hope to see you all at the next Startup School!
